stories.headline: Last U.S. and UK Troops Withdraw from Iraq, Ending Decade-Long Anti-ISIS Mission
stories.summary:
The final British and American troops have departed Iraq, concluding a military presence that began in 2014 as part of the international coalition against the Islamic State. Approximately 100 remaining UK personnel withdrew from Irbil in the northern Kurdistan region in coordination with U.S. forces, fulfilling a withdrawal agreement signed two years ago between Washington and Baghdad. The mission, known as Operation Inherent Resolve, is now formally ended.

Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi marked the departure as Iraq's transition to 'full responsibility for its security and stability,' with the government planning four national 'Sovereignty Days' to commemorate the withdrawal. The Pentagon confirmed the coalition's departure represented 'the successful conclusion of the military mission that defeated IS in Iraq,' while the UK Ministry of Defence noted that Iraqi Security Forces and Kurdish Peshmerga are now positioned to take primary responsibility for the country's security.

Significant security challenges remain. A recent UN report estimated IS retains several hundred fighters still capable of carrying out operations, and Iranian-backed militias — which have resisted Iraqi government efforts at disarmament — could see their influence expand with the U.S. presence gone. Prime Minister Zaidi has vowed to bring all armed factions under state control, but powerful militia groups have so far resisted those efforts.

The withdrawal closes a chapter that began with the 2003 U.S.-led invasion and continued through successive military missions. Hundreds of NATO troops stationed in Baghdad had already departed earlier this year, and the Irbil exit marks the definitive end of the Western military footprint in Iraq.

stories.headline: DHS Tapped $20 Million in Taxpayer Funds for Pro-Trump Campaign-Style Ads Ahead of Midterms
stories.summary:
The Department of Homeland Security used $20 million in taxpayer money — drawn from funds intended for U.S. Customs and Border Protection — to produce and air campaign-style advertisements glorifying President Donald Trump, according to reporting by the Associated Press and Axios. President Trump is personally selecting which ads run, and an administration official told Axios, 'This is just the beginning,' signaling more ads are planned ahead of the November midterm elections.

The White House has characterized the spots as 'public service announcements,' but the seemingly partisan nature of the content has drawn bipartisan condemnation. Critics across the political spectrum, including a senior Republican senator, have called the spending a blatant misuse of public funds that likely violates federal anti-propaganda statutes, which prohibit the executive branch from using appropriated money to produce domestic propaganda.

Democrats have demanded formal investigations and called the ads an abuse of government resources for electoral purposes. A growing number of Republicans have also publicly distanced themselves from the practice, raising questions about legal accountability and oversight of executive spending authority. The controversy arrives five weeks before midterm elections in which control of Congress is at stake.

The episode highlights broader tensions over the Trump administration's use of federal resources in politically charged ways, with legal experts noting that the Anti-Deficiency Act and other statutes may have been violated. No formal legal action has been announced as of Wednesday.

stories.headline: FlyDubai Flight Diverted to Saudi Arabia After Pilots Physically Fight in Cockpit
stories.summary:
A FlyDubai commercial flight traveling from Dubai to Tel Aviv was forced to make an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia on Wednesday after an altercation broke out between the pilot and co-pilot in the cockpit. Both pilots were hospitalized following the incident, which the airline described only as an onboard 'incident' without providing additional details about the nature or severity of the confrontation.

Reports from multiple outlets indicate the two pilots engaged in a violent physical fight mid-flight, prompting the diversion. Saudi Arabian authorities received the aircraft, and passengers were offloaded safely. The flight's emergency landing in Saudi Arabia — a country that only in recent years opened its airspace to Israeli-bound flights — added a geopolitical dimension to what was already an extraordinary aviation safety event.

FlyDubai has not publicly explained what triggered the confrontation or provided an update on the pilots' conditions. Aviation authorities in the UAE and Saudi Arabia are expected to investigate the incident. Physical altercations between flight crew members in the cockpit are extremely rare and represent a serious breach of aviation safety protocols.

stories.headline: Update: Measles Exposures Spread to Trains and Sports Venues as National Outbreak Widens
stories.summary:
The ongoing national measles outbreak has expanded its reach to public transportation and sports venues, health officials confirmed Wednesday, raising new concerns about exposure risks for travelers. Active outbreaks are centered in Pennsylvania, Ohio, and New York, with cases now spanning 47 states. The CDC has previously raised the national death toll to two, and Pennsylvania alone has surpassed 900 confirmed cases.

Health authorities are urging travelers to verify their vaccination status before using planes, trains, or attending large public gatherings, as measles is among the most contagious infectious diseases known and can linger in the air of enclosed spaces for up to two hours after an infected person has left. The MMR vaccine is considered highly effective, providing approximately 97 percent protection after two doses.

The new transportation and venue exposure sites represent a material escalation in the outbreak's geographic spread and transmission risk, particularly for unvaccinated individuals or those with compromised immune systems. Public health officials have stopped short of issuing formal travel advisories but are recommending that anyone without confirmed vaccination history consult a physician.

stories.headline: Trump Signs Voluntary AI Safety Accord with Top Tech Leaders at White House Summit
stories.summary:
President Trump hosted the chief executives of America's largest artificial intelligence companies at the White House on Tuesday, emerging with what he called a "morally binding" voluntary accord on AI safety standards. Signatories include Trump himself alongside Google's Sundar Pichai, Meta's Mark Zuckerberg, OpenAI President Greg Brockman, Anthropic's Dario Amodei, SpaceX's Elon Musk, and Nvidia's Jensen Huang.

Under the agreement, companies take responsibility for ensuring the safety of their own AI systems, committing to implement safeguards, detect and fix unintended behaviors, and work with independent auditors to assess whether their platforms operate as intended. Trump said he would establish a board to oversee AI safety, though he provided no details on its membership or authority. He described the accord as "almost like a constitution, in a way."

Supporters of the deal, including Zuckerberg, said it gives the American public "confidence that the technology works" as intended. Amodei framed it as a way "to win safely." Critics, however, were sharply dismissive. Law professor Kimberlee Weatherall called it "deeply unimpressive," noting the agreement allows firms to "define what counts as safety" and specifies no consequences for breaches. AI governance researcher Jose Miguelito Enriquez said it shows "emerging consensus" but fails to address developer accountability.

The summit comes amid growing international pressure for binding AI regulation and follows a series of AI safety incidents that have heightened scrutiny of the industry's self-policing. The voluntary nature of the accord — with no enforcement mechanism — is the central point of contention between the administration and outside experts who have called for legally enforceable rules.

stories.headline: Update: South Korea Demands North Korea Apologize for DMZ Landmine Blasts That Wounded Three Soldiers
stories.summary:
South Korea's military formally demanded an apology from North Korea on Tuesday after concluding with certainty that landmine explosions in the Demilitarized Zone on September 21 were caused by North Korean mines, wounding three South Korean personnel on South Korea's side of the buffer zone. Seoul called the blasts a clear violation of the 1953 armistice and vowed to take "corresponding measures."

North Korea flatly denied responsibility. Kim Yo Jong, sister of leader Kim Jong Un and one of Pyongyang's most powerful officials, accused Seoul of "cooking up" the claims as a "deliberate and planned strained assertion" to shift blame and escalate tensions. Her statement, published in state media, warned the South to be "prepared for paying a price for the farce of their own making."

South Korean Defence Minister Kang Shin-chul said the mines are believed to have been laid by Pyongyang as part of ongoing efforts to fortify its side of the border. The incident mirrors a 2015 episode in which two South Korean soldiers were maimed by mines in the DMZ, an event Pyongyang also denied. Kim Yo Jong referenced that earlier incident, claiming Seoul had used it as a pretext for escalation then and was doing the same now.

Experts warn the current situation is more volatile than the 2015 confrontation. Crisis Group senior consultant Christopher Green told the BBC that North Korea has been "wilfully attempting to harden the border" and that the two Koreas no longer maintain the low-level communication channels that existed a decade ago. "Accidental escalation on the Korean Peninsula is always just a few steps away, and it's fewer steps now than it was in 2015," he said.

stories.headline: France Detains More Than 400 as Student Protests Over School Conditions Escalate Nationwide
stories.summary:
French authorities detained more than 440 people — the majority of them minors — on Tuesday as student demonstrations over overcrowded classrooms and teacher shortages escalated into violence across the country. Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez confirmed the detentions, noting that roughly two-thirds resulted in formal police custody. At least 400 schools were affected, according to the education ministry.

The unrest, which began in the Île-de-France region around Paris last week, spread to schools across France. Protesters blockaded school entrances, set bins alight, damaged bus stops, and hurled projectiles at police, who responded with batons and tear gas. At least ten teachers, several students, and 48 law enforcement officers were injured during Tuesday's clashes.

"We're here to deliver a message," one 16-year-old student told AFP. "The education system is completely broken. There are 34 of us in each class, and it's just not feasible." Education Minister Édouard Geffray affirmed students' right to protest but condemned the violence as "indefensible," while student union president Ryad Rani accused police of using excessive force and characterized the government's response as "repression."

The student protests coincided with separate nationwide strikes by unions representing teachers, hospital staff, and civil servants over low wages and working conditions, drawing at least 200,000 participants. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu had warned Monday that further escalation would be "irresponsible" after 164 arrests the previous day, but the demonstrations intensified regardless, raising pressure on the government to address underlying grievances in France's public education system.

stories.headline: Morocco Names First Female Prime Minister After Centrist Party Wins Parliamentary Elections
stories.summary:
Fatima Zahra El Mansouri was named Morocco's first female prime minister on Tuesday by King Mohammed VI, following last week's parliamentary elections in which her centrist Authenticity and Modernity Party (PAM) won the most seats. The appointment makes El Mansouri only the second woman to lead a government in the Arab world, after Tunisia's Najla Bouden.

El Mansouri, 50, is a lawyer by training and has served as mayor of Marrakesh since 2009, with an interruption during which she served as a minister overseeing housing and urban planning. She was chosen by the king over PAM's other leading figure, football federation chief Fouzi Lekjaa. Morocco is a constitutional monarchy in which the king retains predominant authority, and the prime minister is appointed by the monarch from the party winning the most seats in parliamentary elections.

El Mansouri has been a prominent figure in Moroccan politics for nearly two decades but has rarely spoken publicly about gender equality or women's rights — topics of active debate in Morocco, including ongoing discussions over polygamy and inheritance law. Asked at a press conference whether state religious ceremonies might need to be modified to accommodate her as head of government, she declined to answer directly, instead praising the king as "the biggest advocate for women" in the country.

With 97 seats, PAM does not hold a majority in parliament and will need to build a coalition government. El Mansouri's appointment is seen as a significant symbolic milestone in a Muslim-majority country in the Arab world, where female heads of government remain exceedingly rare.
